claim: Maximum softmax probability (MSP) is the standard baseline for flagging both misclassified and out-of-distribution inputs, because correct predictions tend to have higher max softmax, but the authors note it can be beaten.
evidence: "Correctly classified examples tend to have greater maximum softmax probabilities"; "the baseline can sometimes be surpassed" (Hendrycks & Gimpel, arXiv:1610.02136)
plain: If the model's top guess has low confidence, that is a cheap first warning that the photo may be wrong or unfamiliar.
project_use: Implement MSP as the zero-cost baseline 'I'm not sure' score that every other method must beat.

claim: The energy score (logsumexp of logits) is a drop-in post-hoc replacement for softmax confidence that reduces average FPR@TPR95 by 18.03% on a CIFAR-10 WideResNet.
evidence: "using the energy score reduces the average FPR (at TPR 95%) by 18.03% compared to the softmax confidence score"; softmax methods "suffer from overconfident posterior distributions for OOD data" (Liu et al., arXiv:2010.03759)
plain: A slightly different formula on the same model outputs catches noticeably more unfamiliar photos than plain confidence.
project_use: Compute energy alongside MSP from the same logits (one line of code) for the OOD test on non-leaf / other-crop photos.

claim: Misclassification detection and OOD detection need different scores: OOD detectors evaluated for selective classification with OOD data rank differently and generally fail to beat the softmax baseline.
evidence: "existing post-hoc methods perform quite differently compared to when evaluated only on OOD detection"; SIRC "is able to consistently match or outperform the baseline for SCOD" while existing OOD methods "fail to do so" (Xia & Bouganis, arXiv:2207.07506)
plain: The best alarm for 'this is not a leaf at all' is not the same as the best alarm for 'I probably got this disease wrong'.
project_use: Report two separate evaluations: AURC/accuracy-vs-coverage on field photos (use MSP) and AUROC/FPR95 for unknown photos (use energy/KNN); possibly combine both scores.

claim: On a fine-grained 8-disease strawberry dataset, open-set methods with outlier exposure detect unknown diseases with AUROC about 0.97, while OpenMax without outlier exposure reached only 70.1% accuracy.
evidence: Two-head network AUROC 0.972, unknown recall 94.9%; OpenMatch AUROC 0.971; "assuming outlier exposure during training is helpful for detecting unknown diseases"; "The outlier exposure provided a significant 16.4% increase in accuracy" (Frontiers in Plant Science 2022)
plain: Showing the model some examples of 'other stuff' during training helps it say 'this is a disease I don't know'.
project_use: If time allows, add an 'other/unknown' outlier set (healthy parts, held-out diseases, random images) during fine-tuning; otherwise hold out 2-3 PlantVillage classes as simulated unseen diseases for evaluation.

claim: Across five public plant-disease datasets, max-logit OOD scoring on a visual-prompt-tuned pretrained model reaches AUROC 94.8% with only 8 shots per class, close to 95.2% with full fine-tuning on all data.
evidence: "the max-logit-based on visual prompt tuning achieves an AUROC score of 94.8% in the 8-shot setting" vs 95.2% full fine-tuning (Dong et al., Scientific Reports 14:17900, 2024)
plain: A big pretrained model needs only about 8 examples per disease to become good at flagging diseases it was never taught.
project_use: Supports using a frozen/lightly tuned pretrained backbone and suggests few expert labels per class may suffice for unknown detection; use max-logit as another free score.

claim: Vision-language (CLIP-style) anomaly detection performs poorly on plant diseases (zero-shot CLIP AUROC 58.47%), and a knowledge-ensemble fix cuts 16-shot FPR@TPR95 from 43.88% to 7.05%.
evidence: "current state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods based on vision-language models perform poorly on plant disease detection tasks"; "reduces the FPR@TPR95 from 43.88% to 7.05%" (16-shot); all-shot 15.38% to 0.71% (Dong et al., Front. Plant Sci. 2025)
plain: General image-text AI models are bad at noticing unfamiliar plant diseases out of the box.
project_use: Do not rely on zero-shot CLIP as the 'not sure' detector; use a fine-tuned image backbone's own scores.

claim: OOD scores can be used as non-conformity scores in conformal prediction, and conformal prediction can correct overly optimistic finite-sample OOD evaluation metrics.
evidence: "evaluation metrics can be overly optimistic due to the finite sample size of the test dataset"; uses "OOD scores as non-conformity scores"; "the two fields may be inherently intertwined" (Novello, Dalmau, Andeol, arXiv:2403.11532)
plain: The same 'strangeness' score that flags unfamiliar photos can be plugged into conformal prediction to give guaranteed-rate warnings.
project_use: Calibrate the OOD threshold conformally on a small expert-labelled field set so the false-alarm rate on known diseases is controlled; report finite-sample uncertainty on FPR95.
